newsitem.title: UK: Man in "punishment shooting" before IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Man in "punishment shooting" before IRA truce.

text.p: A 17-year-old Catholic was shot in both legs in an IRA-style "punishment shooting" hours before the guerrillas' truce was due to take effect, police said on Sunday.

They said the incident happened in the Ballymurphy area of Belfast a few hours after the Irish Republican Army said it was restoring a broken ceasefire at noon on Sunday to win its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at Anglo-Irish peace talks.

The shooting was typical of the kind of violence IRA squads patrolling their own areas hand out to wayward youths every year and which are supposed to stop under British demands for an end to all violence in the province.
The IRA on Satuday said it was calling an "unequivocal restoration" of a broken 1994 ceasefire to its war against British rule of the province.

Britain and Ireland say that if the truce is deemed genuine in a six-week verification period, the IRA's Sinn Fein, led by Gerry Adams, can take part in year-old peace talks from which it has been banned because of IRA violence.

Hours before the truce took effect, hardline pro-British Unionists said they would not negotiate with Sinn Fein at the Belfast peace talks, which meet for a crucial vote on the issue of arms surrender or decommissioning on Wednesday.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, told the BBC: "We would not take part in a process with those who are wedded to violence."
But there was no word from the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) whether it would also walk out of the negotiations between pro-British Unionists and Catholic Irish nationalists.

UUP leader David Trimble was due to meet British Prime Minister Tony Blair in London on Monday to find out under what terms the surrender of the IRA's huge arsenal of automatic weapons and semtex plastic explosive would take place.
The UUP's security spokesman, Ken Maginnis, told GMTV television news that the negotiations would be farcical if it emerged that the British government had done a secret deal with the IRA.

Under British proposals, the handover of guerrilla arms in a 28-year conflict that has killed 3,200 will be negotiated at the same time as a political settlement instead of before the talks start or as part of the final agreement.
"We can't go through into the next century with these people holding the guns at the backs of our heads," Maginnis said.
Maginnis said there were reports that IRA chieftains had been told the truce was only a tactical four-month step to see what Sinn Fein could get at the negotiations.
"Unless we get disarmament, unless we get people committed to consent, we cannot expect that this is going to be other than the farce it was two years ago," he said.
Trimble has urged Blair to allow the talks to go ahead without Sinn Fein until the IRA proves a commitment to democracy by surrendering some of its guns.

Robinson, echoing the UUP line, said the IRA had broken a previous 17-month ceasefire in February last year and there was no guarantee it would not do the same this time if it did not get the kind of political settlement it sought.
"Nobody can believe the IRA because they had a previous cessation which was proved to be phoney," he said.
But John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, a moderate Irish nationalist group, urged all Unionists to accept that violence had ended with the IRA truce.
"Decommissioning is one of the biggest red herrings we have ever had. Where in the world where you have a conflict does a solution begin with decommissioning," he told the BBC.
"They (the IRA) could hand over 1,000 guns on Monday and buy 1,000 more on Tuesday. The real question is to get the violence stopped," he said.
Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein''s chief negotiator, told GMTV that Unionists feared change and urged them to take part in the talks to bring about a lasting settlement.

"If we get into these talks, if we go there with good will on all sides, wanting peace desperately, wanting to bring about the peace that is required, then I think we can bring about a situation where we will have a permanent peace on this island eventually," he said.
